title: Impression materials & disinfection
blurb: Alginate, silicones and polyethers: choosing the tray, mixing well, and getting an accurate, disinfected impression to the lab.
question: The dentist has just taken an alginate impression for a partial denture and the lab courier is not due until tomorrow. Another patient's alginate impression came back from the lab last week full of small bubbles. What should you do with today's impression, and what probably caused last week's bubbles?

teach.body: An impression is a negative copy of the teeth and soft tissues. The lab pours it with gypsum (dental plaster or stone) to make a positive copy: the cast or model. Every crown, denture, orthodontic appliance and mouthguard starts here. If the impression is distorted, torn or full of bubbles, the finished work will not fit. Your job is to pick and try in the tray, mix the material correctly, and then rinse, disinfect, package and label the impression for the lab.

children.label: Elastic
children.sub: Flex out of undercuts, then recover

teach.caption: Rigid materials suit edentulous ridges with no undercuts. Wherever there are teeth, an elastic material is needed.

teach.h: Why elastic materials win when teeth are present
teach.body: Teeth bulge wider at the contact points than at the gum, so there are undercuts. A rigid material would lock in, then fracture or distort on removal. An elastic material stretches past the bulge and springs back to its set shape. Alginate is the everyday elastic choice for study models, opposing models, orthodontics, whitening trays and dentures. Elastomers (addition silicone and polyether) are used when accuracy really matters, such as crowns, bridges, inlays and implants.

items: Try in the tray, then apply the silicone tray adhesive and let it dry.
Bleed the cartridge: express a little until both pastes flow evenly.
Fit a new mixing tip (a set tip is blocked and cannot be reused).
Load the tray, and pass the syringe of light-body wash to go around the preparation.
Seat the tray and hold it still for the full setting time.

teach.text: Alginate is mostly water. Left out to dry it loses water and shrinks (syneresis); left soaking it absorbs water and swells (imbibition). Never leave it on the side or in a pot of water. Disinfect it, then wrap it in damp (not wet) gauze in a sealed bag and get it poured as soon as possible.

steps.sub: Removes disinfectant that could affect the cast

steps.sub: Sealed bag; lab ticket notes it is disinfected

teach.caption: Use a disinfectant the material's manufacturer approves. Polyether must not be left soaking, or it swells.

items: Rigid materials (compound, ZOE paste) suit edentulous mouths; elastic materials are needed when teeth create undercuts.
Alginate: room-temperature water, thorough spatulation, load without trapping air, pour quickly.
Addition silicone is the most accurate and stable choice for crowns: bleed the cartridge and use a new tip each time.
Try the tray in first for fit, extension and comfort, use the right adhesive, and don't overload it: excess material runs back and makes the patient gag.
Every impression is rinsed, disinfected, rinsed, bagged and labelled before it goes to the lab.

summary: You can now classify impression materials as rigid or elastic, explain why teeth with undercuts need an elastic material, mix and load alginate without faults, prepare an automix silicone in the right order, and rinse, disinfect and package any impression safely for the laboratory.

A.q: The dentist reports large voids in an alginate impression. What is the most likely cause?
options: The tray had too many perforations
Air was trapped during mixing or loading
The water used was slightly too cold
The impression was left in disinfectant too long
A.why: Voids come from air whipped into the mix or trapped as the tray is loaded. Firm spatulation against the bowl and pressing the mix into the tray prevent them.

whyNot.0: Perforations help retain the material; they don't create voids in the impression surface.
whyNot.2: Cold water slows the set and gives more working time; it doesn't cause voids.
whyNot.3: Over-disinfecting may affect the surface, but it doesn't create bubbles from trapped air.

A.q: The dentist needs a highly accurate impression of a crown preparation that may not be poured until tomorrow. Which material is most suitable?
options: Alginate
Impression compound
Zinc oxide eugenol paste
Addition silicone
A.why: Addition silicone is very accurate and dimensionally stable, so it can be poured later and even poured more than once.

whyNot.0: Alginate is not accurate enough for crown work and changes shape if pouring is delayed.
whyNot.1: Impression compound is rigid and used for edentulous primary impressions, not crown preparations.
whyNot.2: ZOE paste is rigid and used as a wash in special trays for edentulous mouths.

A.q: An alginate impression has just been removed from the mouth. What should happen first?
options: Rinse it under running water
Wrap it straight in dry paper towel
Spray it with disinfectant at once
Put it in a pot of water to keep it moist
A.why: Rinsing removes saliva and blood so the disinfectant can then work on a clean surface.

whyNot.1: Dry paper would draw water out of the alginate and it would shrink (syneresis).
whyNot.2: Disinfectant works poorly through saliva and blood, so the impression is rinsed before disinfection.
whyNot.3: Soaking in water makes alginate swell (imbibition) and distorts the model.

B.q: Mixed alginate looks grainy, with specks of dry powder. What is the best explanation?
options: The tray adhesive was not dry
The water was too warm
It was not spatulated enough
The powder was fluffed first
B.why: A grainy mix means the powder and water were not fully combined. Alginate needs vigorous spatulation against the side of the bowl until smooth.

whyNot.0: Wet adhesive affects how the set impression sticks to the tray, not the texture of the mix.
whyNot.1: Warm water speeds up the set; it doesn't leave dry powder in the mix.
whyNot.3: Fluffing (shaking) the tub before measuring is correct practice and gives accurate scoops.

B.q: Before loading an automix addition silicone cartridge, what should you do?
options: Re-use the tip from the last impression
Express a little paste until both flow evenly
Warm the cartridge in hot water so it flows better
Mix the pastes by hand on a glass slab
B.why: Bleeding the cartridge makes sure both base and catalyst are flowing evenly, so the material mixes in the right ratio once the tip is fitted.

whyNot.0: A used tip contains set material, so it is blocked and cannot mix correctly. Use a new tip.
whyNot.2: Heat speeds up the set and shortens working time; it is not part of preparing a cartridge.
whyNot.3: The whole point of an automix cartridge is that the tip mixes it; hand mixing defeats that.

B.q: Why does an edentulous patient's impression sometimes use a rigid material, while a patient with teeth needs an elastic one?
options: Rigid materials set much faster in the mouth
Elastic materials don't stick to soft tissues
Rigid materials can only be used in stock trays
Teeth create undercuts rigid materials can't pass
B.why: Teeth are wider at the contact points than at the gum, so a rigid material would lock in and break or distort on removal. Smooth edentulous ridges have no such undercuts.

whyNot.0: Setting speed isn't what decides it; the issue is whether the set material can be removed past undercuts.
whyNot.1: Elastic materials record soft tissue well; alginate is used for many denture impressions.
whyNot.2: ZOE paste is often used in a special (custom) tray, not a stock tray.

C.q: During try-in, the stock tray rocks and doesn't cover the last molars. What is the best action?
options: Load extra material to fill the gap at the back
Ask the patient to bite down on the tray
Use a faster-setting alginate instead
Choose a better-fitting tray before mixing
C.why: A tray that rocks or misses the molars will give an incomplete impression, so a better-fitting tray must be chosen before any material is mixed.

whyNot.0: Overloading won't record the missed area and makes gagging more likely.
whyNot.1: Biting on the tray will distort the impression and doesn't fix poor extension.
whyNot.2: Setting speed doesn't fix a tray that is the wrong size.

C.q: Which statement about polyether impression material is correct?
options: It is the cheapest choice for study models
It sets by evaporation of water
It is very accurate but swells if soaked
It is a rigid material for edentulous ridges
C.why: Polyether is a highly accurate elastomer, but it absorbs water, so it must not be left immersed in disinfectant or water.

whyNot.0: Alginate is the low-cost choice for study models; polyether is used for precision work.
whyNot.1: Polyether sets by a chemical reaction between base and catalyst, not by drying.
whyNot.3: Polyether is elastic, though quite stiff once set.

C.q: A disinfected alginate impression cannot be poured for several hours. How should it be stored?
options: In a sealed bag with damp gauze
Open on the bench to air dry
Submerged in a cup of water
In the medicines fridge, uncovered
C.why: A sealed bag with damp (not wet) gauze limits water loss or gain. Even so, alginate should be poured as soon as possible.

whyNot.2: Soaking makes alginate absorb water and swell (imbibition).
whyNot.3: The medicines fridge is for medicines only, and uncovered alginate would still dry out.

reteach.title: Think of alginate like a jelly
reteach.question: If you made a jelly and left it out overnight, or dropped it in a bowl of water, what would happen to its shape?

blocks.body: Set alginate is a gel full of water, a bit like a jelly. Leave a jelly uncovered and it shrinks and cracks as water evaporates. Sit it in water and it swells and goes soft. Alginate does exactly the same, and a model poured from a shrunken or swollen impression won't fit the mouth. That's why alginate is rinsed, disinfected, kept in a sealed bag with damp gauze, and poured as soon as possible. Silicones are rubbery, not watery, so they stay the same shape for much longer.

blocks.text: Memory hook: SyneResis = Shrinks as water is Released. IMbibition = takes water IN.

explain.body: Rigid materials (impression compound, zinc oxide eugenol paste) can't bend, so they are only used where there are no undercuts, mainly edentulous ridges. Elastic materials (alginate, silicones, polyether) flex past undercuts and recover, so they are used whenever teeth are present.

test.q: Which impression material is classed as rigid?
options: Alginate hydrocolloid
Polyether elastomer
ZOE impression paste
Addition silicone
test.why: ZOE impression paste sets hard and can't flex past undercuts, so it is used as a wash for edentulous impressions.

whyNot.1: Polyether is an elastic elastomer, though stiff.
whyNot.3: Addition silicone is an elastic elastomer.

explain.body: Fluff the powder, use level scoops and the measured water at room temperature. Spatulate firmly against the side of a flexible bowl until the mix is smooth and creamy, then press it into the tray so no air is trapped. Warm water makes it set too fast; too little spatulation leaves it grainy.

test.q: An alginate mix sets before the dentist can seat the tray. What is the most likely cause?
options: The water was too warm
The tray was perforated
The powder was fluffed
The bowl was flexible
test.why: Warmer water speeds up the alginate setting reaction and cuts working time.

whyNot.1: Perforations retain the material and don't affect setting.
whyNot.2: Fluffing gives accurate measuring and doesn't speed the set.
whyNot.3: A flexible bowl is the correct equipment for mixing alginate.

explain.body: Addition silicone is very accurate and stable, so it is the usual choice for crowns and bridges. It comes in putty, heavy-body and light-body; the light-body wash is syringed around the preparation. Hand-mixed putty can fail to set if handled in latex gloves, and the material needs a dry field. Polyether is also very accurate, but stiff and swells if soaked.

head: Consistency
Job
rows: Bulk in the tray; hand or machine mixed
Syringed round the prep for fine detail
explain.caption: Handle hand-mixed putty in non-latex gloves: latex can stop it setting.

test.q: The impression tore around deep undercuts when it was removed. Which material property was not good enough?
options: Setting time
Tear strength
Working time
Heat resistance
test.why: Tear strength is how well a set material resists tearing as it is pulled past undercuts. Alginate's is low; elastomers' is much better.

whyNot.0: Setting time is how long it takes to set, not how it behaves on removal.
whyNot.2: Working time is how long you have to load and seat it.
whyNot.3: Heat resistance isn't relevant to removing an impression from the mouth.

explain.h: Disinfect before it leaves the surgery
explain.body: Every impression is a cross-infection risk to lab staff. Rinse off saliva and blood under running water, disinfect with an impression disinfectant for the manufacturer's contact time, rinse again, then seal in a labelled bag. The lab ticket (the dentist's written prescription) should state that it has been disinfected.

test.q: What is the correct order for preparing an impression for the laboratory?
options: Disinfect, bag, rinse and then label
Bag, rinse, disinfect and then label
Rinse, disinfect, rinse, bag and label
Label, disinfect, bag and then rinse
test.why: Rinsing first removes saliva and blood, disinfection then works on a clean surface, and a final rinse removes disinfectant before it is sealed and labelled.

whyNot.0: Disinfecting before rinsing means saliva and blood shield microbes from the disinfectant.
whyNot.1: It can't be rinsed or disinfected once it is sealed in a bag.
whyNot.3: Rinsing must come before disinfection, and the impression is bagged last.
